researched_by: the Authority's own visitor pages and online shop, Natural Resources Wales' site page for a car park the Authority manages, the Authority's 2024-25 draft statement of accounts, local-democracy reporting of the May 2026 planning applications for parking machines, and park4night field reports
policy_summary:
The opposite of the Peak District in almost every respect. Where that Authority owns 44 car parks and closes every one of them by byelaw, Bannau Brycheiniog owns roughly eight, has no byelaws that anyone publishes, and relies entirely on signage, rangers and the fact that most of its car parks are too small or too awkward for a motorhome to get into.

The first thing to establish is that almost nothing a visitor associates with this park belongs to the Authority. Pen y Fan's main car park at Pont ar Daf is the NATIONAL TRUST - rebuilt with 180-plus spaces, GBP 7.50 for non-members, and its own explicit no-overnight rule. The Storey Arms lay-bys on the A470 are trunk-road land. The forest car parks (Blaen y Glyn, Pont Melin Fach, Garwnant) are Natural Resources Wales, which says flatly that 'overnight parking is not allowed at any NRW site'. Talybont and Pontsticill reservoirs are Welsh Water. Llangorse Lake's lakeside parking is the private Lakeside Caravan and Camping Park; Talybont-on-Usk's is the village hall. Brecon, Hay, Crickhowell, Abergavenny and Llandovery town car parks are Powys, Monmouthshire or Carmarthenshire. Four or five separate regimes can apply within a mile.

What the Authority actually owns is: the National Park Visitor Centre (the Mountain Centre) at Libanus; Craig y Nos Country Park in the upper Swansea Valley; the two official Waterfall Country car parks, Cwm Porth and Gwaun Hepste, above Ystradfellte; Keeper's Pond and Fox Hunter on the Blorenge road above Blaenavon; the Llyn-y-Fan road car park at Llanddeusant; and the Carreg Cennen car park at Trapp. The first four are pay and display - GBP 2 to GBP 3 at the Visitor Centre, GBP 6 a car in Waterfall Country, card only. The last four are free.

On overnight use the position is consistent but thinly evidenced. The clearest published statement is not on the Authority's own site at all: NRW's page for Gwaun Hepste, which it states is 'a pay and display car park, managed by the Bannau Brycheiniog National Park Authority', says in terms 'Overnight parking is not permitted.' On the ground the same rule is enforced at Keeper's Pond, a well-known free upland stop until about 2021, where van users now report 'no camping' signs and National Park rangers moving people on. The Authority's camping page directs everyone to designated campsites and states that wild camping is 'illegal without the landowners permission'. No car park opening or closing hours are published for any Authority site, and no byelaw was found - so the prohibition is a landowner's rule backed by signage, not an offence.

The two Waterfall Country car parks carry a restriction that matters more to a large van than the night rule does: both are 'not available for large vehicles which cannot access the parking site - ie motorhomes, coaches or caravans will block the busy, single lane roads'. The busiest site in the Authority's ownership is closed to motorhomes by day as well as by night.

There is NO provision of any kind. No aire, no designated bays, no chemical or grey-water disposal, no motorhome facilities at any Authority site. The only reference to overnight vehicles anywhere in the Authority's published material is to send you to a commercial campsite.

The direction of travel is monetisation rather than prohibition, and it is driven by insolvency. The Authority needs about GBP 5.227m a year and receives about GBP 4.528m from Welsh Government grant and local authority levies; officers have warned it could exhaust reserves and 'go bust by 2029'. Its response has been to go after parking income - the Waterfall car park cost centre already returned a GBP 64k net surplus in 2024-25 - and in spring 2026 it applied for planning permission to install donation-and-fee machines at four of its free car parks. The Llyn-y-Fan road and Carreg Cennen applications were approved by its own planning committee on 19 May 2026; the two Blaenavon ones, inside the World Heritage Site, were held for a heritage impact assessment after Cadw asked for more detail. The description of development expressly includes future car parking fees, so the free upland car parks are on a path to becoming charged ones - and a tariff is the mechanism by which hours, and then a closure, usually arrive.
notes:
Read the rebrand as a research hazard, not a curiosity. The park became Bannau Brycheiniog in April 2023, but the Authority still trades on beacons-npa.gov.uk, still calls its online shop 'Brecon Beacons National Park Shop', and every historic document, planning list and press release says Brecon Beacons. Search under both names or you will miss half the record.

The most useful single finding is negative: this Authority has no car park byelaws that can be found. Peak District, Dartmoor and the Lake District all have them; Bannau Brycheiniog appears to have none, and its car parks are not covered by any traffic regulation order either, because they are its own land rather than highway. That means a van in an Authority car park at 2am is not committing an offence in the way it would be at Tideswell Dale. It is a trespasser once asked to leave, and nothing more. The practical consequence is that enforcement depends on a ranger physically turning up - which, judging by the Keeper's Pond reports, they do, but only where there is a known problem.

The Waterfall Country large-vehicle exclusion is the sharpest real-world constraint in this file and it is geometric rather than legal. The lanes to Cwm Porth and Gwaun Hepste are single track; the Authority's position is that a motorhome will block them. Anyone planning to base a large van on Ystradfellte should be reading that sentence, not the overnight rule.

The ownership map is the thing a human is most likely to get wrong here, and it is worth being blunt about it. Pont ar Daf, which is what almost everyone means by 'the Pen y Fan car park', is National Trust and belongs in national-trust.json - it has 180-plus spaces, a section open 24 hours for mountain access, and an explicit ban on overnight stays, which is exactly the sort of record that would be misfiled here. Cwm Gwdi is also National Trust. Gwaun Hepste sits on NRW land in Coed y Rhaiadr but is run by the Authority, so its record belongs here and not in an NRW file - a genuinely ambiguous case resolved by NRW's own wording.

The financial trajectory is the thing to watch. An authority that is one bad year from insolvency and has just won permission to put machines in its remaining free car parks is not going to leave those car parks unmanaged overnight indefinitely. If a formal closure or an overnight charge appears anywhere in this park in the next two years, Keeper's Pond and Fox Hunter are where it will appear first.

OWN-PROVISION SWEEP, 27 July 2026 - NIL RETURN, AND CRAIG Y NOS IS SETTLED. The obvious candidate for hidden provision here was Craig y Nos Country Park, which the Authority genuinely does own and manage and which appears above only as a car park record. THERE IS NO CAMPING, CARAVANNING OR MOTORHOME PROVISION AT CRAIG Y NOS. Two independent sources say the same thing: the Authority's own country park page describes a forty-acre Victorian garden with a visitor centre and tea room open 10:00 to 16:30, and the Fforest Fawr Geopark page confirms it is 'owned and managed by the Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons) National Park Authority' with no camping, caravan or campervan facility mentioned. It is a day park that shuts in the afternoon.

The name causes a specific confusion worth killing here: CRAIG-Y-NOS CASTLE, next door, is a privately run hotel and events venue and is not the Authority's. Anyone who has heard of 'camping at Craig y Nos' is thinking of the castle grounds or of a nearby private or club site, not the country park.

The Authority's own camping page confirms the wider negative. It carries no Authority-run site at all and says only that 'we encourage visitors to use designated campsites', listing farm-based and commercial operators. So the finding of the main file - no provision of any kind, no aire, no bays, no disposal point - survives the step-2 check that was designed to break it. Every campsite in this national park belongs to somebody else: private farms, Natural Resources Wales at Coed y Rhaiadr, Blaen y Glyn, Pont Melin Fach and Garwnant, the National Trust at Pont ar Daf and Cwm Gwdi, and the two caravan clubs.
open_questions: Does the Authority have any confirmed byelaws at all - for its car parks, or for Craig y Nos Country Park under the Countryside Act 1968? None was found in any search, which is itself notable for a national park authority, but absence of evidence is not proof.

Is any Authority car park physically gated or locked overnight? Craig y Nos Country Park publishes hours of 10am to 4.30pm and the Visitor Centre 10am to 4pm, but neither page says whether the car park closes with them. No opening_hours restriction is recorded because none could be verified.

Is the 'Llyn-y-Fan road car park, Llanddeusant' named in the May 2026 planning application the main walkers' car park at the head of the road (recorded here) or a lower one nearer the village? The application description gives no grid reference.

Were the Keeper's Pond and Fox Hunter machine applications approved after the Cadw-requested heritage impact assessment? Both sit inside the Blaenavon Industrial Landscape World Heritage Site and were still undetermined when reported.

Does Cwm Porth carry the same explicit 'overnight parking is not permitted' wording as Gwaun Hepste? Only the NRW page for Gwaun Hepste states it; the Authority's own waterfalls page is silent on the night.

There is no published inventory of Authority car parks. Eight are recorded here from scattered sources; there may be others, particularly small roadside pull-ins in the Black Mountains and on Mynydd Illtud.
What penalty, if any, follows a refusal to move on? No fixed penalty, PCN or prosecution route was found for Authority land.

sites.name: Gwaun Hepste Car Park, Waterfall Country
sites.search_hint: Gwaun Hepste car park, Ystradfellte waterfalls
sites.notes: THE ONE EXPLICIT PUBLISHED PROHIBITION IN THIS FILE, and it is on someone else's website. NRW's page for the site says 'Gwaun Hepste is a pay and display car park, managed by the Bannau Brycheiniog National Park Authority' and then 'Overnight parking is not permitted.' The land is NRW's, in Coed y Rhaiadr forest; the operation and the rule are the Authority's. GBP 6 a car, GBP 7 a minibus, and the ticket machine takes cards only. The larger of the two official Waterfall Country car parks but with no toilets or shop - those are at Cwm Porth. Separately and importantly, the Authority states the site is 'not available for large vehicles which cannot access the parking site - ie motorhomes, coaches or caravans will block the busy, single lane roads', so a motorhome is excluded by day as well as by night.

sites.name: Cwm Porth (Porth yr Ogof) Car Park, Ystradfellte
facilities: shop selling snacks, drinks and souvenirs, open daily
sites.search_hint: Cwm Porth car park, Four Waterfalls walk, Ystradfellte
sites.notes: The Authority's flagship car park and the busiest site it owns - the start of the Four Waterfalls walk, full by 9.50am on a summer Sunday according to its own 2020 press release, and redeveloped at a cost of GBP 79k in 2024-25. GBP 6 a car, card only. The recorded restriction here is the vehicle-size one, which is explicit and in force: 'Not available for large vehicles which cannot access the parking site - ie motorhomes, coaches or caravans will block the busy, single lane roads.' A motorhome should not attempt the lanes at all. No overnight statement is published for Cwm Porth specifically, but the Authority's rule at its sister car park Gwaun Hepste is that overnight parking is not permitted and there is no reason to think this site is treated differently. When Cwm Porth fills, visitors are directed to private farm overflow fields which take cash only and are not the Authority's - do not read this record across to them.

sites.name: Keeper's Pond (Pen-ffordd-goch) Car Park, B4246 above Blaenavon
sites.search_hint: Keeper's Pond car park, B4246, Blaenavon
sites.notes: The best-documented enforcement in this file, and it comes from van users rather than the Authority. A free upland car park by the pond with big views to the Sugar Loaf and Abergavenny, listed on park4night with 40 reviews, it was a tolerated overnight stop until around 2021. Reviews from 2021 onward consistently report 'no camping' signs and National Park rangers enforcing them; the listing is now marked as overnight prohibited. No byelaw, no fixed penalty and no published Authority statement - signage and a ranger visit are the whole mechanism. Confirmed as Authority-owned in the reporting of the 2026 parking machine applications, which describe all four sites as car parks the Authority owns. A donation-and-fee machine is proposed here; the application was undetermined pending a Cadw heritage impact assessment because the site is inside the Blaenavon Industrial Landscape World Heritage Site. Daytime problems are real too - full by 10am, noise and litter.
sites.geocode_precision: park4night pin on the car park itself, corroborated by the OpenStreetMap position of Keeper's Pond at 51.7915, -3.0814 immediately north

sites.name: Fox Hunter Car Park, Blorenge, B4246 near Blaenavon
sites.search_hint: Foxhunter car park, Blorenge, opposite the twin aerial masts, B4246
sites.notes: Free car park on the Blorenge above Blaenavon, named for the showjumper Foxhunter whose ashes are buried nearby, reached by the turning opposite the twin aerial masts. Confirmed as an Authority-owned car park in the reporting of the spring 2026 parking machine applications, which named Fox Hunter and Keeper's Pond alongside Llyn-y-Fan road and Carreg Cennen as 'car parks it owns'. The overnight position is INFERRED, not published: it sits a kilometre from Keeper's Pond, is managed by the same rangers, and the Authority's line everywhere it has stated one is that overnight parking is not permitted. Confidence is low precisely because no sign, statement or field report was found for this specific site. Like Keeper's Pond it is inside the Blaenavon World Heritage Site and its machine application was held for a Cadw heritage impact assessment.
sites.geocode_precision: OS grid reference SO 263 107 published as the walk start point, converted OSGB36 to WGS84; the same source quotes 51.790536, -3.069918

sites.name: Llyn-y-Fan road car park, Llanddeusant
sites.search_hint: Llyn y Fan Fach car park, Llanddeusant, Llangadog
sites.notes: The walkers' car park for Llyn y Fan Fach and the Carmarthen Fans, at the end of a single-track road with few passing places and no facilities of any kind. Free at present. Confirmed as Authority-owned: its planning committee approved an application on 19 May 2026 to install a donation-and-fee machine and signage here, by seven votes to nil with one abstention, the officer stating the machine would 'collect donations and car parking fees' with the potential for actual charging built into the description of development. NOTE THE OWNERSHIP TRAP - Welsh Water owns the reservoir works and access track further up the valley, and the upper filter-bed track is not the Authority's. No overnight statement is published for this car park; the restriction recorded here is inferred from the Authority's position elsewhere and is low confidence. The single-track approach makes it a poor motorhome proposition regardless.

sites.search_hint: Carreg Cennen car park, Trapp, Llandeilo
sites.notes: A free car park about 250 metres north of Carreg Cennen Castle, in the far west of the park. The castle itself is Cadw's and is run with a working farm and its own visitor facilities - this car park is the Authority's, confirmed by its planning committee's approval on 19 May 2026 (six for, one against, one abstention) of a donation-and-fee machine and signage here. No overnight statement is published; the restriction is inferred from the Authority's position elsewhere and is low confidence. Approached by narrow lanes from Trapp.

sites.name: National Park Visitor Centre (Mountain Centre) car park, Libanus
facilities: toilets including accessible and Changing Places
six EV charging points (standard, not rapid)
sites.search_hint: Bannau Brycheiniog National Park Visitor Centre, Libanus, Brecon
sites.notes: The Mountain Centre on Mynydd Illtud Common, five minutes off the A470 at Libanus - wholly owned and managed by the Authority and the only site it runs with a full set of facilities. Pay and display: GBP 2 up to four hours, GBP 3 over four hours, free for blue badge holders, cash, card or phone; an annual permit is GBP 40, or GBP 55 jointly with Craig y Nos. The centre itself opens 10am to 4pm daily. An overflow field opens at peak times. NO CAR PARK OPENING OR CLOSING TIME IS PUBLISHED and no overnight rule is stated on the Authority's own page, so the restriction recorded here is inferred from its position at Gwaun Hepste and Keeper's Pond - low confidence, and worth a phone call before relying on it either way. Physically this is the most van-friendly site the Authority has: level tarmac, no height barrier reported, toilets, cafe and EV points. That makes the absence of a published rule more of a live question here than anywhere else in the file.
sites.geocode_precision: OS grid reference SN977262 for the Mountain Centre, quoted with decimal coordinates 51.924984, -3.488565 and matching an independent OSGB36 conversion to 51.92489, -3.48907

sites.name: Craig y Nos Country Park car park, Pen-y-cae
sites.search_hint: Craig y Nos Country Park, Brecon Road, Pen-y-cae, Swansea Valley
sites.notes: The historic grounds of Craig-y-Nos Castle in the upper Swansea Valley, owned and managed by the Authority as a country park and a Registered Historic Park and Garden. Large pay and display car park, tarmac and compacted stone, free for permit and blue badge holders, with EV charging; the annual permit is GBP 40 or GBP 55 jointly with the Visitor Centre. Coaches are not taken in the main car park and must drop off at the layby by the top entrance. The country park is published as open 10am to 4.30pm every day. WHETHER THE CAR PARK IS PHYSICALLY GATED OUTSIDE THOSE HOURS IS NOT STATED ANYWHERE and is the single most consequential unknown in this file - if it is, that would be a genuine opening_hours closure of the sort the Peak District applies by byelaw. It is recorded here as a policy restriction only, at low confidence, because nothing was found to confirm a gate. Note also that as a country park designated under the Countryside Act 1968 this is the one Authority site where byelaws would be a natural instrument; none was found. The park was closed for a period after extensive storm damage in December 2024 and received GBP 105k of capital works in 2024-25.
sites.geocode_precision: OS grid reference SN 840155 published for the country park, converted OSGB36 to WGS84; an independent mapping pin for the park gives 51.82552, -3.68067

sites.name: All Bannau Brycheiniog National Park Authority car parks - overnight parking and sleeping
sites.notes: The estate-wide position, assembled rather than quoted, because the Authority does not publish a parking policy page. The evidence is: NRW's page for Gwaun Hepste, which the Authority manages, stating 'Overnight parking is not permitted'; consistent field reports of 'no camping' signs and ranger enforcement at Keeper's Pond since about 2021; and the Authority's camping page, which offers no vehicle option at all and directs everyone to designated campsites. NO BYELAW AND NO TRAFFIC ORDER WAS FOUND covering any Authority car park - these are its own landholdings, not highway, so the rule is a landowner's rule. That has a practical consequence worth understanding: unlike the Peak District, where staying past midnight is a criminal offence carrying a level 2 fine, here there is no offence and no penalty charge, only a trespass once you have been asked to leave. Enforcement is a ranger arriving in person. Recorded at medium confidence because the rule is consistent everywhere it is stated but is stated in very few places.

sites.name: Wild camping and overnight sleeping on land within the National Park
sites.notes: The Authority's camping page states that 'Wild camping, though appealing, is illegal without the landowners permission' and that 'Most land in the National Park is privately owned, with specific uses like farming or conservation', which makes permission hard to get. It asks visitors to use designated campsites, and makes a point of the farm-based ones supporting the rural economy. This is a restatement of the general law of trespass rather than an instrument of the Authority's own - and it matters more here than in the English parks because Bannau Brycheiniog owns very little land. There is no equivalent of the Peak District's blanket 'we do not allow wild camping on any land that we own', because there is barely any such land to speak of beyond the eight car parks, Craig y Nos and Mynydd Illtud.
